power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: With the global decline in adolescents' reading skills over the decade, reading-related anxiety begins to draw increasing attention.
Over time, the potential feedback loop of higher anxiety and poorer reading may block pathways to academic achievements and increase the likelihood of health problems.
This study examined multi-dimensional nature of reading anxiety using a sample of 654 Finnish students in Grades 7-9.

The students self-assessed reading anxiety, reading control and values (utility, interest, and importance values), and reading frequency of traditional texts (e.g., book, magazine, newspaper) and digital texts (e.g., social media contents).
First, confirmatory factor analysis suggested three components of reading anxiety across genders and grades, i.e., physiological and affective, cognitive, and motivational reading anxiety.
Second, latent (hierarchical) regressions and difference testing further supported differences among the reading anxiety components.
Lower reading control and higher reading values were associated with higher reading anxiety.
Reading anxiety was also associated with reading frequency.
However, cognitive reading anxiety appeared to be an essential component in terms of the overall stronger associations with reading control, values, and traditional texts reading frequency.
Furthermore, reading anxiety and reading frequency association direction were variable.
More frequent traditional reading was associated with higher cognitive reading anxiety, but lower physiological and affective reading anxiety (among girls) and motivational reading anxiety.
More frequent digital reading was related to higher motivational reading anxiety (among boys).
The findings are practically meaningful for supporting identification and regulation of reading anxiety and in turn promoting reading engagement and skills and well-being among young people.
Reading plays an essential role in academic learning and achievement (e.g., OECD, 2010).

text.text: The global decline in adolescents' reading skills over the past decade requires more attention to reverse this alarming trend (OECD, 2026).
text.formatted: The global decline in adolescents' reading skills over the past decade requires more attention to reverse this alarming trend <ref type="bibr">(OECD, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In this study, we focus on one critical but largely understudied aspect of reading: anxiety related to reading situations (hereafter referred to as reading anxiety).
Compared with other forms of academic anxiety (e.g., math anxiety, test anxiety), reading anxiety only begins to draw increasing attention in recent years.
Concerningly, reading anxiety appears to emerge already in early grades (e.g., Cui et al., 2026; Ramirez et al., 2019), and is generally associated with poor reading skills (Johnson et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Concerningly, reading anxiety appears to emerge already in early grades (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cui et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Ramirez et al., 2019)</ref>, and is generally associated with poor reading skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Johnson et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Over time, reading anxiety and skills can be reciprocally linked with each other (Ramirez et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Over time, reading anxiety and skills can be reciprocally linked with each other <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ramirez et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The potential feedback loop of higher anxiety and poorer reading may block pathways to academic achievements and increase the likelihood of physical health problems (Pekrun et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The potential feedback loop of higher anxiety and poorer reading may block pathways to academic achievements and increase the likelihood of physical health problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Pekrun et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: At present, the fundamental question of the nature of reading anxiety is yet to be thoroughly addressed.

Herein, this study aims to investigate whether reading anxiety is a multidimensional construct among adolescents through identifying its underlying components and examining how these components are associated with reading control, reading values, and voluntary reading frequency.
Overall, reading plays a vital part across subjects learning and diverse academic situations.
To investigate the nature of reading anxiety, we use the control-value theory (CVT; Pekrun, 2006; 2017; 2021) as the framework for this study.
text.formatted: To investigate the nature of reading anxiety, we use the control-value theory (CVT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Pekrun, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">2021)</ref> as the framework for this study.

text.text: CVT was proposed to explain academic emotions and their associations with self-appraisals, learning engagement, and performance.

In CVT, general academic anxiety is considered a negative and physiologically activating emotion in response to academic learning situations (e.g., attending classes, engaging in learning tasks, and taking tests) that are subjectively important, which typically includes affective (uneasy and nervous feelings), physiological (bodily symptoms), cognitive (performance worries), and motivational (impulses of task avoidance) components.

Following the CVT logic of general academic anxiety, we hypothesize that reading anxiety can also be conceptualized as a multi-dimensional construct, that would include multiple components of anxiety related to reading situations.

Empirically, reading anxiety has been often assessed as a single-dimensional construct by adapting scales originally created to measure other forms of academic anxiety, such as children's math anxiety (Chung et al., 2024; Pollack et al., 2021; Grills et al., 2026), university students' foreign language anxiety (Tang et al., 2021), or general academic anxiety (Clem et al., 2021; Lauermann et al., 2017; Päivinen et al., 2019; Prinz-Weiß et al., 2023; Sainio et al., 2021; Zaccoletti et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Empirically, reading anxiety has been often assessed as a single-dimensional construct by adapting scales originally created to measure other forms of academic anxiety, such as children's math anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Chung et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Pollack et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Grills et al., 2026)</ref>, university students' foreign language anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Tang et al., 2021)</ref>, or general academic anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Clem et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lauermann et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Päivinen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Prinz-Weiß et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sainio et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Zaccoletti et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Limited studies examined the multi-dimensionality of reading anxiety in terms of its sources.

For example, an early study among English-speaking Grades 4-6 students conceptualized reading anxiety as a phobia-like reaction to reading, however, their measure also tapped reading motivation-related constructs (Zbornik & Wallbrown, 1991).
text.formatted: For example, an early study among English-speaking Grades 4-6 students conceptualized reading anxiety as a phobia-like reaction to reading, however, their measure also tapped reading motivation-related constructs <ref type="bibr">(Zbornik & Wallbrown, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Next, a recent study among Turkish Grade 5-8 students examined reading anxiety along the lines of reading stages: before, during, and after reading (Sümer Dodur & Ceylan, 2025).
text.formatted: Next, a recent study among Turkish Grade 5-8 students examined reading anxiety along the lines of reading stages: before, during, and after reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Sümer Dodur & Ceylan, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, Jones et al. (2025) referred to the research on associations of poor reading with general anxiety and social anxiety and found three factors for reading anxiety among English-speaking Grade 7-12 students: anxiety experienced in general reading, anxiety experienced when reading aloud, and reading anxiety-related physiological symptoms.
text.formatted: Finally, <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Jones et al. (2025)</ref> referred to the research on associations of poor reading with general anxiety and social anxiety and found three factors for reading anxiety among English-speaking Grade 7-12 students: anxiety experienced in general reading, anxiety experienced when reading aloud, and reading anxiety-related physiological symptoms.

text.text: These studies, stemming from different theoretical perspectives, have shed light on sources of reading anxiety.

To complement the existing perspectives and inform identification and regulation of reading anxiety, it is also imperative to ask about the multidimensionality of reading anxiety, specifically in how it manifests.

Factor analyses of other forms of academic anxiety, specifically math anxiety among upper elementary and secondary schools' students, frequently assessed and identified the affective (nervous feeling) and cognitive (performance worry) components (e.g., Grade 4, Henschel & Roick, 2017; 2020; Grade 6, Ho et al., 2000; Grade 6-12, Wigfield & Meece, 1988).

text.text: According to CVT (Pekrun, 2006; 2017; 2021), domain-specific academic anxiety (such as reading anxiety) proximally depends on low control combined with high value appraisals.
text.formatted: According to CVT <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Pekrun, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">2021)</ref>, domain-specific academic anxiety (such as reading anxiety) proximally depends on low control combined with high value appraisals.

text.text: Applying CVT to reading situations, the control appraisal implies that reading tasks can be performed and desired outcomes can be achieved.

For value appraisal, students may highly value reading because it is important to them to be a good reader (importance value), useful to read well to attain other goals (utility value), and interesting to them (interest value).
It would follow that students may develop reading anxiety when they feel uncertain about being able to read and understand what they read, while reading well is subjectively valued.

It is further theorized that repeated experiences of having a lack of control, indicated by individuals' low self-efficacy belief in performing specific tasks and achieving expected outcomes (Bandura, 1977), will be generalized to low ability self-concept belief over time (Pekrun, 2021).

text.text: In this study, we focus on reading control indicated by self-efficacy but also review studies on ability self-concept as the two related constructs have both been used in the literature.

In general, empirical studies among upper elementary and secondary schools' students found that high reading anxiety was associated with low reading self-efficacy and ability self-concept (e.g., Chinese Grade 8, Chung et al., 2024; Finnish Grade 6, Clem et al., 2021; Italian Grade 5, Zaccoletti et al., 2020).

text.text: Insights into the potential multi-dimensionality of reading anxiety might be gained from math anxiety literature.
One study among elementary and secondary students showed that cognitive and affective math anxiety positively related to math task effort amount (Grades 6-12, Wigfield & Meece, 1988).

text.text: Specifically, invested effort amount had a moderate correlation with cognitive worry and a weak correlation with nervous feelings.

Studies on math anxiety and math performance in the similar age groups suggested that both the association directionality and strength differed between cognitive and affective math anxiety (e.g., Grade 4, Henschel & Roick, 2017; Grade 6, Ho et al., 2000; Grade 2-5, Sorvo et al., 2017; 2019; Grades 6-12, Wigfield & Meece, 1988).

text.text: Given the lack of research into the potential multi-dimensional manifestation of reading anxiety, we considered the studies on anxiety related to particular subject learning (math) and academic situations (attending classes, engaging in learning tasks, and taking tests) to shed light on the topic.
However, the findings may not be generalizable across domains (e.g., Lauermann et al., 2017).
text.formatted: However, the findings may not be generalizable across domains (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lauermann et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike particular subject learning such as math and academic situations such as test taking that typically involve specific problems solving with straightforward and consequential assessment feedback, reading is inevitable and fundamental across subjects learning and academic situations, but may not always come with straightforward performance evaluation.
As such, the nature of anxiety related to reading (i.e., structure and associations with correlates) may not be the same as that of anxiety related to particular subjects or academic situations.
Supporting identification and regulation of reading anxiety is crucial for promoting young people's reading engagement and skills and well-being.
To enable this, we need to deepen understanding of the nature of reading anxiety.
Our current study investigates multi-dimensional reading anxiety in Grades 7-9 (age 14-16) in Finland.
Specifically, we ask the following research questions: 1) Are there physiological, affective, cognitive, and motivational components within reading anxiety?
2) Are reading anxiety components differentially associated with reading control, values, and reading frequency?
Taken together the theoretical assumptions and research on reading anxiety and other forms of academic anxiety, we formulate the following hypotheses.
First, we expect to identify multiple components of reading anxiety, which may include physiological, affective, cognitive, and motivational reading anxiety.
Second, reading anxiety components are hypothesized to show some differences in the associations with reading control, values, and reading frequency.

Considering control and values appraisals, reading anxiety can be associated with low reading control and high reading values, particularly high importance and utility values, but the associations' strength might differ between reading anxiety components.
For reading anxiety and reading frequency, negative and positive association can be both possible, and the association strength might differ between reading anxiety components.

text.text: This study belonged to the evaluation of easy language books donation to lower secondary schools project.
The current data was collected in spring 2025, consisting of 654 Grades 7-9 students (49.5% girls) from secondary schools in different regions of Finland.
Of the participants, 170 (26%) were in Grade 7, 339 (52%) were in Grade 8, and 144 (22%) were in Grade 9.
Finnish was the native language of most students (N=578, 89.1%).
The study was assessed by the Ethics Committee.
Informed consent was obtained from adolescent participants, and students' guardians were notified before the study.
The web-based anonymous questionnaire (REDCap) was in the Finnish language and distributed to the students via their teachers.
The students read the questions in the questionnaire themselves and answered on their own.
Reading anxiety was measured using the "Multi-Dimensional Reading Anxiety Scale" (Table 1).
text.formatted: Reading anxiety was measured using the "Multi-Dimensional Reading Anxiety Scale" (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: This is a self-report scale, the use of which is supported by previous reading anxiety research showing that adolescents' self-reports are comparable with parent-reports (e.g., Jones et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This is a self-report scale, the use of which is supported by previous reading anxiety research showing that adolescents' self-reports are comparable with parent-reports (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Jones et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The scale includes 12 items being rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = I do not feel like this at all,5 = I feel like this very much), with 3 items measuring each of the four theoretical components of reading anxiety (i.e., physiological, affective, cognitive, and motivational).
We adapted item No. 2, 7, 9 from an existing reading anxiety scale for adolescents (Jones et al., 2025) and item No. 1, 4, 6 from a math anxiety scale (Sorvo et al., 2017; 2019).
text.formatted: We adapted item No. 2, 7, 9 from an existing reading anxiety scale for adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Jones et al., 2025)</ref> and item No. 1, 4, 6 from a math anxiety scale <ref type="bibr">(Sorvo et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2019)</ref>.

text.text: We created the other items based on academic anxiety (Pekrun et al., 2005) taking into account general reading, reading aloud, and independent reading in silence situations that are common among adolescents.
text.formatted: We created the other items based on academic anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Pekrun et al., 2005)</ref> taking into account general reading, reading aloud, and independent reading in silence situations that are common among adolescents.

text.text: The items measuring the theoretical components showed adequate internal consistency (Cronbach's Alpha =.70 for physiological, .74 for affective, .85 for cognitive, and .79 for motivational reading anxiety).

Reading control was assessed by a measure of self-efficacy, including 7 questions asking students to evaluate how confident they are that they can perform the given reading tasks (4-point Likert scale,1 = I definitely can't,4 = I'm absolutely sure I can, Cronbach's Alpha = .94).
The items were adapted from Peura et al. (2021).
text.formatted: The items were adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Peura et al. (2021)</ref>.

text.text: Reading values included utility, interest, and importance values.

For each value, one question asked students how much they perceive the utility of reading, interest in reading, and importance of reading, respectively (5-point-Likert scale,1 = Not at all,5 = Very much) (Aunola & Nurmi, 1999; Nurmi & Aunola, 2005).
text.formatted: For each value, one question asked students how much they perceive the utility of reading, interest in reading, and importance of reading, respectively (5-point-Likert scale,1 = Not at all,5 = Very much) <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aunola & Nurmi, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Nurmi & Aunola, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Reading frequency was assessed by 6 items asking students how often they voluntarily read traditional texts (e.g., books, magazine, newspaper, Cronbach's Alpha = .79) and 3 items asking how often they voluntarily read digital texts (e.g., contents on social media, blogs, emails, Cronbach's Alpha = .74; 5-point Likert scale,1 = Never or hardly ever,5= Several times a week).
Five items for traditional texts were from OECD (2019) and the other items were developed in the project.

text.text: Descriptive statistics were computed by IBM SPSS 30.0.0.0.
The observed items displayed some skewness.
Item missingness ranged from 0.2 -13.5%.
Little's MCAR test suggested that the missingness may be completely at random (χ2 (1450) = 1487.59, p = .24).
The main analysis was conducted in Mplus 8.11 (Muthén & Muthén, 1998 -2017).

text.text: We used the maximum likelihood estimation with robust standard errors (MLR) for handling non-normal distribution and full information maximum likelihood (FIML) for handling missingness.

To address the first research question, we applied confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to test the four component factors model (i.e., physiological, affective, cognitive, and motivational reading anxiety) and hierarchical model with the components being first-order factors and reading anxiety as a secondorder factor.
Reading anxiety measurement invariance across genders and grades was tested using multigroup CFA with chi-square difference testing.
To address the second research question, we used structural equation modeling (SEM).
First, separate CFA tested the measurement model for reading control and reading frequency.
Second, separate latent regressions tested reading anxiety components in relation to reading control and values and reading frequency.
For evaluating the models' fit, the chisquare goodness-of-fit test can be sensitive to large sample sizes.

The fit of the tested models to data was indicated by: the root-mean-square error of approximation (RMSEA) < .08, standardized root mean residual (SRMR) < .08, comparative fit index (CFI) and Tucker-Lewis index (TLI) > .90 (Browne & Cudeck, 1993; Hu & Bentler, 1999).

text.text: The measures mostly approximated normal distribution and there were no extreme outliers.
However, some of the reading anxiety items showed positive skewness and digital reading frequency displayed negative skewness.
Bivariate correlations (Table 3) showed that not all the reading anxiety components had statistically significant correlations with reading control, values, and reading frequency.

To address the first research question, we applied CFA to test the four component factors model (i.e., physiological, affective, cognitive, and motivational reading anxiety) and hierarchical model with the components being first-order factors and reading anxiety as a second-order factor.
See Supplemental material B for the models' fit statistics.

Although the CFA supported the four component factors model, it did not support the hierarchical model, which seemed to be related to physiological and affective reading anxiety factors being strongly correlated (r = .99).

Additional analysis using graded response modeling further revealed that both physiological and affective anxiety in general reading were experienced by those with a rather high reading anxiety trait level (+1.5 SD) (see full results in Supplemental material C).
Thus, the four-component models of reading anxiety were rejected.

Once physiological and affective reading anxiety were combined into one factor, CFA supported both the three component factors model and hierarchical model (Fig. 1, see Supplemental material B for fit statistics) suggesting that the items measure a latent reading anxiety factor that has three latent subcategories.

text.text: Then, multigroup CFAs with chi-square difference testing were run to establish measurement invariance across genders and grades.

The results suggested that the three component factors model of reading anxiety was similarly established across genders and grades with equal item factor loadings and intercepts (see Supplemental material B).
Gender and grade level differences were found in reading anxiety factors mean.
Girls were higher than boys on all of the reading anxiety components, and 7 th graders showed a higher level of motivational reading anxiety than 8 th and 9 th graders.
Thus, gender and grade were included as covariates in the following SEM.
To address the second research question, we first tested the measurement model for reading control (source) and reading frequency (outcome).
Reading values of interest, importance, and utility were single items and therefore included in SEM as observed variables.

Separate CFAs suggested a single-factor structure for reading control and a two-factor structure for reading frequency (traditional reading and digital reading) with measurement invariance being reasonably established between genders (see Supplemental Tables SD1-SD2).
text.formatted: Separate CFAs suggested a single-factor structure for reading control and a two-factor structure for reading frequency (traditional reading and digital reading) with measurement invariance being reasonably established between genders (see Supplemental Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">SD1-SD2</ref>).

text.text: There were no gender differences in the mean level of reading control and traditional reading, however, girls read more digital texts than boys.
In the following two sections, we report the full SEM results for reading anxiety in relation to reading control and values (sources), and traditional and digital reading frequency (outcome).
Gender and grade were included as covariates in each SEM.

To test whether reading control and three task values explained variance in reading anxiety, three sets of latent regression models were constructed (Fig. 2), specifically, Model 1 for control and utility value, Model 2 for control and interest value, and Model 3 for control and importance value.

text.text: In each set of Models 1-3, we tested additive effects of control and values (Models 1A-3A) and control X value interactive effect (Models 1B-3B) on reading anxiety.
In all the models, control and value were allowed to covary.
Residual covariances between reading anxiety components were included.
The variables were standardized before including interactions, except for gender and grade.
The models fit well with the data (see fit statistics in Supplemental Table SD3).

text.text: Overall, lower reading control was associated with higher reading anxiety (with only one exception for motivational reading anxiety in Model 2A).
Higher utility and importance values of reading were associated with higher reading anxiety, while interest value was not related to reading anxiety.
Additionally, control X value interactions were all significant (Fig. 3).

text.text: Lower reading control was associated with higher reading anxiety, particularly when reading was highly valued.

Then, difference testing compared the unconstrained (control and value predictive paths freely estimated) with the constrained model (control and value predictive paths fixed equal across reading anxiety components in Models 1A-3A, and control X value interaction paths fixed equal across components additionally in Models 1B-3B).
The results supported that reading anxiety components differed in the association strength with reading control and values (Supplemental Table SD3).

text.text: Separate Wald tests comparing the significant control and value predictive paths in Models 1A-3A (Table 4) indicated that overall, cognitive reading anxiety, relative to motivational reading anxiety, showed a stronger negative association with reading control.

text.text: Also, cognitive reading anxiety, relative to the other reading anxiety components, showed stronger positive associations with reading utility and importance values.

Multigroup analyses suggested gender moderated the associations of reading anxiety with reading control and values (see Supplemental material D-Gender Difference Analyses, Table SD4-SD6). For boys, higher reading anxiety was consistently related to higher reading values, but not lower reading control or lower control X high values.

In general, the results were in line with those of the whole group analysis, with one additional finding in that for boys, cognitive reading anxiety, relative to motivational reading anxiety, also showed a stronger positive association with reading interest value.

To examine the unique variance in reading frequency explained by each reading anxiety component, we conducted 3 sets of latent hierarchical regressions (Models 4-6, Fig. 4 5 6) using Cholesky decomposition of the intercorrelations between reading anxiety components (de Jong, 1999).

text.text: Different orders of entering predictors were tested in each set of hierarchical regression.

We constructed Models 4A-4B for unique variance explained by physiological and affective reading anxiety, Models 5A-5B for unique variance explained by cognitive reading anxiety, Models 6A-6B for unique variance explained by motivational reading anxiety.

For example, in Model 4A for physiological and affective reading anxiety, three phantom factors (i.e., shared_cognitive, residual_motivational, residual_physiological and affective reading anxiety) were created to capture, respectively: 1) the shared variance of cognitive reading anxiety among reading anxiety components, 2) the residual of motivational reading anxiety when cognitive reading anxiety was partialled out, and 3) the residual of physiological and affective reading anxiety when cognitive and motivational reading anxiety were partialled out.

text.text: The results indicated that reading anxiety components differed in the strength and direction of their associations with traditional reading frequency.

After controlling for the respective other reading anxiety components, traditional reading frequency was associated with cognitive reading anxiety positively and motivational reading anxiety negatively, but not with physiological and affective reading anxiety.
Specifically, when cognitive reading anxiety was included, physiological and affective and motivational reading anxiety were not associated with traditional reading.
Whereas, when motivational reading anxiety was considered, the cognitive reading anxiety-traditional reading positive association remained.

Additional reading anxiety components differences were revealed by Models 4-6 multigroup analyses with separate Wald tests comparing the significant coefficients for the unique associations of reading anxiety components with reading frequency (see Supplemental material D gender difference analyses).
For girls, physiological and affective reading anxiety was uniquely and negatively related to traditional reading.
For boys, motivational reading anxiety was uniquely and positively related to digital reading for boys (though such gender difference was not statistically significant).

However, for boys none of the reading anxiety components explained unique variance of traditional reading after accounting for the positive associations of the respective other reading anxiety components with traditional reading.
To support identification and regulation of reading anxiety, we need to first deepen our understanding of the nature of reading anxiety.
Using a sample of Finnish adolescents in Grades 7-9 (age 14-16), the study provided evidence for the multi-dimensional reading anxiety.
First, there were three components of reading anxiety across genders and grades, i.e., physiological and affective reading anxiety, cognitive reading anxiety, and motivational reading anxiety.

Second, the three reading anxiety components were differentially associated with the theoretical sources (reading control, reading values of interest, importance, and utility) and outcome (traditional and digital texts reading frequency).

From our CFA results, students experiencing reading anxiety may have various responses to reading -both physiological and psychological -including perceived bodily symptoms and uneasy feelings (physiological and affective reading anxiety), thoughts worrying about performance and evaluation (cognitive reading anxiety), and avoidance tendencies (motivational reading anxiety).
This partially supported our first hypothesis that there are different components in reading anxiety, similar to, but slightly deviating from general academic anxiety.
In the literature on general academic anxiety (Pekrun et al., 2002; 2011), four distinct components were identified, with physiological and affective components being separate components.
text.formatted: In the literature on general academic anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Pekrun et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2011)</ref>, four distinct components were identified, with physiological and affective components being separate components.

text.text: Conversely, we did not find physiological component was differentiated from affective component, such that for reading anxiety, perceived bodily symptoms were closely associated with uneasy feelings.
Our finding of physiological and affective reading anxiety being one component instead of two may be understood from the nature of emotional responses and reading situations.

On one hand, the systematic review on physiological arousal of emotional responses suggested that physiological reaction level may depend on the situation, e.g., heart rate increases particularly when encountering situations that involve acute threat and require quick responses (Scherer & Moors, 2019).
text.formatted: On one hand, the systematic review on physiological arousal of emotional responses suggested that physiological reaction level may depend on the situation, e.g., heart rate increases particularly when encountering situations that involve acute threat and require quick responses <ref type="bibr">(Scherer & Moors, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this view, compared to anxiety related to attending classes and engaging in learning tasks, it was reported that university students' perceived physiological arousal level was overall higher for anxiety related to tests taking, which typically comes with straightforward and consequential evaluations and strict time limit for responses (Pekrun et al., 2002).

text.text: Also, in another study the four components (physiological, affective, cognitive, and motivational) were better differentiated in anxiety related to test-taking than in anxiety related to attending classes and engaging in learning tasks (Pekrun et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Also, in another study the four components (physiological, affective, cognitive, and motivational) were better differentiated in anxiety related to test-taking than in anxiety related to attending classes and engaging in learning tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Pekrun et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Turning to reading for lower secondary school students in the context of our study, typical situations such as reading for subject learning and assignments may not always come with straightforward evaluations and strict time limit for responses.

Reflected in the current analyses of reading anxiety items, bodily symptoms (headache, body tension) related to reading in general were often experienced only by students with elevated reading anxiety (+1.5 SD).

On the other hand, some theorists propose that the affective component of emotions can be a complex conglomerate of central integrated representation of the other emotional components, while some emphasize the role of perception of bodily changes in subjective feelings formation, implying a close link between physiological and affective components (Scherer, 2009).
text.formatted: On the other hand, some theorists propose that the affective component of emotions can be a complex conglomerate of central integrated representation of the other emotional components, while some emphasize the role of perception of bodily changes in subjective feelings formation, implying a close link between physiological and affective components <ref type="bibr">(Scherer, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The current analyses of the reading anxiety items also suggested that both physiological and affective reactions of anxiety in general reading situations were typically experienced among students having severe reading anxiety (+1.5 SD).

It is plausible that for reading situations in general, students may interpret perceived bodily symptoms (e.g., tension and headache) as them experiencing uneasy feelings related to reading, particularly when these symptoms are noticed frequently.

In addition to the evidence from CFA, the separate latent regressions further supported our second hypothesis for multi-dimensional reading anxiety in terms of the theoretical sources (reading control and values) and outcome (reading frequency) of reading anxiety (Pekrun, 2006; 2017; 2021; Pekrun & Linnenbrink-Garcia, 2012).
text.formatted: In addition to the evidence from CFA, the separate latent regressions further supported our second hypothesis for multi-dimensional reading anxiety in terms of the theoretical sources (reading control and values) and outcome (reading frequency) of reading anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Pekrun, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Pekrun & Linnenbrink-Garcia, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In line with the unidimensional reading anxiety literature (e.g., Chung et al., 2024; Clem et al., 2021; Lauermann et al., 2017; Zaccoletti et al., 2020), we found that low reading control and high reading values (particularly utility and importance values) were associated with reading anxiety.
text.formatted: In line with the unidimensional reading anxiety literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Chung et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Clem et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lauermann et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Zaccoletti et al., 2020)</ref>, we found that low reading control and high reading values (particularly utility and importance values) were associated with reading anxiety.

text.text: Meanwhile, lower reading control was associated with higher reading anxiety, particularly when reading was highly valued.
Furthermore, reading anxiety was associated with reading frequency.
Together, the above evidence suggested that the identified three components (physiological and affective, cognitive, and motivational) were underlying reading anxiety phenomenon.
Importantly, differences among the reading anxiety components were found in the following two aspects.
First, overall, cognitive reading anxiety had stronger associations with reading control, reading value of utility, interest, importance, and reading frequency of traditional texts.
The findings indicated that cognitive worry about reading performance better captured reading anxiety.

In other words, cognitive worry appeared to be an essential component of reading anxiety, which could be plausible considering reading anxiety proximal sources being cognitive appraisals-control and values (Pekrun, 2006; 2017; 2021; see also test anxiety, Roos et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In other words, cognitive worry appeared to be an essential component of reading anxiety, which could be plausible considering reading anxiety proximal sources being cognitive appraisals-control and values <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Pekrun, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see also test anxiety, Roos et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For reading situations, students may evaluate whether they are able to read well and whether it is important to read well.
The cognitive appraisals result of low control and high value of reading may be easily connected with worrisome thoughts about not being able to read fluently and comprehend reading materials.
Second, reading anxiety and reading frequency association direction were variable.

Specifically, higher cognitive reading anxiety was associated with more traditional texts reading, while higher physiological and affective reading anxiety (among girls) and higher motivational reading anxiety were associated with reduced traditional reading.

Our finding extends unidimensional reading anxiety literature in that previous studies focused mainly on affective and physiological reading anxiety and documented its negative association with reading frequency (Edwards et al., 2023; Salins et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Our finding extends unidimensional reading anxiety literature in that previous studies focused mainly on affective and physiological reading anxiety and documented its negative association with reading frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Edwards et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Salins et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Based on our results, worrisome thoughts about reading performance appeared to be important for efforts investment in voluntary reading of traditional text materials such as books, magazines, newspapers.

Considering the similar finding in the math anxiety literature (e.g., Wigfield & Meece, 1988), it is likely that a certain level of worry about reading may be indicative of a gap between students' current reading skills and desired reading performance.
text.formatted: Considering the similar finding in the math anxiety literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Wigfield & Meece, 1988)</ref>, it is likely that a certain level of worry about reading may be indicative of a gap between students' current reading skills and desired reading performance.

text.text: This gap may motivate students to invest effort in reading practice to avoid failures.

To further understand the variable associations between reading anxiety and reading frequency, we will need to consider the interplays of reading anxiety and control and values appraisals (Pekrun, 2006; 2017; 2021).
text.formatted: To further understand the variable associations between reading anxiety and reading frequency, we will need to consider the interplays of reading anxiety and control and values appraisals <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Pekrun, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">2021)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, it is likely that students' worry about reading performance may motivate their reading practices particularly when reading is important for them.

Experienced bodily symptoms and uneasy feelings related to reading might lower perceived control over performing reading tasks and achieving expected outcomes, and in turn, discourage reading practices.
Moreover, the variable associations of reading anxiety with reading frequency may be also related to how reading frequency is assessed.
Extending the literature on reading anxiety and reading frequency (Edwards et al., 2023; Salins et al., 2026), we separately assessed reading frequency of traditional and digital texts.
text.formatted: Extending the literature on reading anxiety and reading frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Edwards et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Salins et al., 2026)</ref>, we separately assessed reading frequency of traditional and digital texts.

text.text: We found that reading anxiety in the specific form of avoidance tendencies (among boys) was related to increased digital texts reading.

In contrast to the traditional texts reading (e.g., magazines, books, newspapers), digital texts reading (e.g., social media contents) typically features shorter texts with more visual information, and thus can be an easier option for those who are anxious about reading and display avoidance tendencies.
However, more digital reading may be associated with poorer reading comprehension over time (e.g., Torppa et al., 2020).
text.formatted: However, more digital reading may be associated with poorer reading comprehension over time (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Torppa et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: To better understand reading anxiety associations with reading frequency, future studies should consider not only how much students read but also what and how they read.
The current findings have practical implications for reading anxiety identification and regulation.

To facilitate regulation, we first need to know more about reading anxiety symptoms, which not only include affective and physiological responses, but also cognitive and motivational reactions to reading situations.

While some students may not verbalize their anxious feelings nor experience bodily symptoms related to reading, they may have worries about reading performance and making mistakes and attempt to escape from reading.
In literacy instruction and learning, careful attention is needed for activities that may prompt students' reading competence appraisals and reading anxiety.

For example, group reading activities may facilitate students' reading via peer collaborations and support but might also put stress on some students, who will be concerned about making mistakes in front of others and falling behind peers and thus be reluctant to participate.
To understand students' anxious reactions to reading, open communication between teachers and parents and students may be helpful.

To support reading anxiety regulation, it may be useful to target anxious reactions together with its sources, e.g., reading motivational beliefs and reading skills (Cui et al., 2026; Dolean, et al., 2026; Ramirez et al., 2019), as boosting reading skills and shaping typical motivational beliefs can take time (e.g., Aro et al., 2018; Lovett et al., 2021).
text.formatted: To support reading anxiety regulation, it may be useful to target anxious reactions together with its sources, e.g., reading motivational beliefs and reading skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cui et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Dolean, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Ramirez et al., 2019)</ref>, as boosting reading skills and shaping typical motivational beliefs can take time (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Aro et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Lovett et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Based on the evidence for different reading anxiety components, students may be guided in understanding functional importance of their emotional reactions (Scherer, 2009) and be explicitly taught how to recognize and interpret their mental and bodily symptoms related to reading as signals of preparing themselves for engaging in important and meaningful learning with texts.
text.formatted: Based on the evidence for different reading anxiety components, students may be guided in understanding functional importance of their emotional reactions <ref type="bibr">(Scherer, 2009)</ref> and be explicitly taught how to recognize and interpret their mental and bodily symptoms related to reading as signals of preparing themselves for engaging in important and meaningful learning with texts.

text.text: Meanwhile, relaxation strategies instruction may help students reduce their bodily reactions in reading situations (James et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Meanwhile, relaxation strategies instruction may help students reduce their bodily reactions in reading situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(James et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, the study was among the first to investigate the multi-dimensionality of reading anxiety.

To examine this emerging topic, we started with exploring how students' perceived reading anxiety typically look like and how their perceived reading anxiety relates to reading-related self-appraisals and behavioral reading engagement.
We applied a cross-sectional design with self-report measures in a relatively large sample across Finnish secondary schools.
However, the study is not without limitations.
Self-report bias cannot be eliminated.
Also, students' reading-related appraisals and anxious reactions may fluctuate over time and situations.

Future studies may zoom into dynamics of reading anxiety (embodying physiological and affective, cognitive, and motivational reactions) and its interplays with reading-related self-appraisals in learning with texts.

To this end, self-report of typical traits may be considered with methods, such as experience sampling method capturing perceptions changes, devices registering respiration and heart rate indicating physiological states, log file data and eye-tracking monitoring behavioral engagement in reading.
In addition, gender difference in reading anxiety was not the current focus and thus not thoroughly examined, but some findings are important to be noted.
Based on our multigroup analyses, for boys, higher reading anxiety was associated with more traditional texts reading and the association was not much differentiated among reading anxiety components.
Also, lower reading control was not consistently associated with higher reading anxiety for boys.

To further understand the nature of reading anxiety and related gender differences so as to support reading anxiety regulation, future studies may examine proximal sources of reading anxiety beyond control and values appraisals (Pekrun, 2021).
text.formatted: To further understand the nature of reading anxiety and related gender differences so as to support reading anxiety regulation, future studies may examine proximal sources of reading anxiety beyond control and values appraisals <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Pekrun, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For boys, reading anxiety might be experienced when they find challenges in reading for learning that is important to them, but they are not certain about closing the gap between the existing reading skills and desired learning outcomes.
If the appraisal focus is on the existing skills gap more than incompetence self-belief, they might try to close the gap by increasing reading practices.
Alongside the global decline in adolescents' reading skills (OECD, 2026), reading anxiety begins to draw increasing attention in recent years (Johnson et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Alongside the global decline in adolescents' reading skills (OECD, 2026), reading anxiety begins to draw increasing attention in recent years <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Johnson et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The present study contributed to our knowledge of the nature of reading anxiety, which is meaningful for supporting identification and regulation of reading anxiety among young people and in turn promoting reading engagement and skills and well-being.

Based on the evidenced multi-dimensional reading anxiety, we suggest educators and families observing and communicating with students about reading anxiety symptoms and providing students with knowledge and skills of recognizing and regulating the symptoms alongside reading motivation and skills support.

For instance, it may be helpful to provide explicit instructions on recognizing the importance of emotional reactions, using relaxation strategies to calm the body, and interpreting reading-related physiological and psychological responses as signals of preparing for important learning.

To move forward, future research may examine the nature of reading anxiety in terms of its self-appraisal sources beyond control and values and its influences on reading engagement from both quantitative and qualitative perspectives.

Also, it is important to understand dynamic interplays of reading-related self-appraisals and anxiety (involving cognitive, motivational, and affective and physiological reactions) in learning with texts.

text.formatted: To complement understanding of reading anxiety components in terms of items properties, we applied graded response model (GRM)-a generalized two-parameter logistic model <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Samejima, 1969)</ref>.

text.text: For each reading anxiety component, GRM estimated individual reading anxiety items discrimination α and difficulty β parameters, category response curves CRCs, and item information curves IICs.

In Mplus, the two-parameter logistic model with reading anxiety factors variance set to one and factors mean set to zero, presented factor model parameterization (i.e., item loading and threshold), which were then converted to the conventional GRM parameterization (i.e., item discrimination and difficulty) (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2020).
text.formatted: In Mplus, the two-parameter logistic model with reading anxiety factors variance set to one and factors mean set to zero, presented factor model parameterization (i.e., item loading and threshold), which were then converted to the conventional GRM parameterization (i.e., item discrimination and difficulty) <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Asparouhov & Muthén, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For the current 5-point Likert scale measuring reading anxiety, GRM estimated the probabilities of lower versus higher response categories in a dichotomy form, i.e., selecting category 1 versus category 2,3,4,5; category 1,2 versus category 3,4,5; category 1,2,3 versus category 4,5, and category 1,2,3,4 versus category 5 (Embretson & Reise, 2000).

text.text: The category response curves CRCs representing response probability of each category conditional on reading anxiety latent trait level were estimated by computing differences between probability of responding to a lower category and higher category.

The CRCs shapes and locations were determined by two types of parameters, i.e., one discrimination (slope) parameter α and four difficulty (location) parameters β1, β2, β3, β4 (the number of response categories minus one).
CRCs can be transformed to item information curves IICs, which indicate the amount of psychometric information each item can provide across latent trait levels (Baker, 2001; Embretson & Reise, 2000).

text.text: To interpret the GRM parameters, the larger item α parameter estimate (α < 0.65 as low, 0.65-1.34 as moderate, 1.35-1.69 as high, and > 1.70 as very high) and the narrower and peaked the CRCs indicate the better item discrimination across latent trait levels, i.e., category response probabilities change fast alongside the change of trait level (Baker, 2001).

text.text: Gender moderated the associations of reading anxiety with reading control and values.
Low reading control was more consistently related to high reading anxiety among girls, but was only related to high cognitive reading anxiety among boys in Models 2A-3A.

For girls, high utility and importance values of reading were related to high cognitive reading anxiety, while high interest value was related to low physiological and affective and motivational reading anxiety.
For boys, high utility, interest, and importance values were associated with high reading anxiety regardless of components.

text.text: For a given item, a large β1 value indicates a high trait level required to have .50 probability of selecting above Category 1 (I do not feel like this at all) and a large β4 indicates a high trait level required to have .50 probability of selecting Category 5 (I feel like this very much).

Negative and smaller β values indicate "easy" items that function among those at lower end of trait level, while positive and larger β values indicate "difficult" items that function among those at higher end of trait level.
Overall, β parameters estimates distributed across latent trait continuum indicate items can well capture individuals at varied trait levels.

IICs shapes and locations were also determined by discrimination α and difficulty β parameters, with a larger α parameter estimate corresponding to a higher IIC peak, and more dispersed β parameters estimates corresponding to a wider latent trait range an item can measure with precision.

IICs can be summing up together to form test information curve TIC which indicates the latent trait range (falling close to the curve peak) where the entire scale items can measure with precision and less standard error of measurement.
